entries.summary: Our new integrations let AI agents reason across Oracle’s business-critical data. The post Microsoft and Oracle bring agentic AI into flow of enterprise work appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog.
entries.text: This blog is co-authored by Arpan Shah, SVP of Oracle Databases and Muneer Mirza, VP of Multicloud at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Today at Microsoft Ignite, we’re bringing agentic AI into the flow of enterprise work. Our new integrations let AI agents reason across Oracle’s business-critical data—from finance and supply chain to HR and customer operations—and the work context Microsoft Work IQ understands across meetings, email, documents, and Teams. Customers can access this combined intelligence through Excel, Teams, and Microsoft Copilot. Built on Oracle AI Database@Azure, the integrations help businesses turn trusted enterprise data into insights and actions, with the choice, security, and performance mission-critical workloads demand. Learn more about Oracle on Azure With Oracle AI Database@Azure, Oracle and Microsoft have helped customers modernize critical workloads to improve application performance and unlock more value from their enterprise data, by bringing databases closer to applications and connecting enterprise data with Microsoft AI. Oracle AI Database@Azure now spans 33 Azure regions, more than on any other hyperscaler, delivering the performance and flexibility customers need. entries.summary: At Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’ll showcase what’s possible when models, silicon, and cloud infrastructure converge into a single, co-engineered system.
entries.text: The top announcements: AKS and Microsoft Foundry Azure Catalyst Windows Server 2028 As AI continues to reshape how every business builds, operates, and competes, it is rapidly emerging as the defining workload in the cloud. This new class of agents, more demanding, complex, and dynamic than anything before them, is rewriting the rules of cloud infrastructure. Reasoning across multi-agent systems, drawing on rich context, acting in real time, and running continuously, they ask more of every layer of the platform beneath them. This week, we’re introducing innovations across Microsoft Azure that set a new standard for how the cloud powers AI: expanded AI core capabilities in Azure to build what’s next, and Azure Catalyst, an intelligent agent-led solution to modernize the apps, data, and infrastructure that already run the business. For years, we have been reengineering every layer of Azure for the unique demands of AI and proving it on the world’s most advanced AI workloads, from leading frontier models to our own GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft 365. That work has forged Azure into a single, co-engineered system, with models, silicon, and cloud infrastructure tuned as one and value compounding at every layer. This week, we take that even further. Over the past year, my conversations with customers have changed. A year ago, the question was which model to choose. Now it’s how to put agents to work on the processes that run the business, and how to trust them to do it. With the same frontier models available to everyone, the advantage comes from what no one else has: your context. It’s how your business runs, what your people know, and the systems and data you’ve spent years building. That’s your IQ. It’s your intellectual property, so it should stay yours, and it should work wherever your people and agents do. Our job is to make every layer beneath your agents better, from the infrastructure that runs them and the estate they act on to the apps they power and the business context that tells them how your company works. Azure is the foundation of Frontier Transformation. entries.summary: Azure Cobalt 200 VMs bring improved performance and efficiency to cloud-native applications, databases, developer tools, and agentic AI workloads.
entries.text: Today at Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re announcing the general availability of Azure Cobalt 200-based virtual machines (VMs). Cobalt 200 VMs deliver up to 50% better performance than Cobalt 100 and are now available in 14 regions, expanding to 23 regions by the end of 2026. Built for cloud-native, data-intensive, and agentic AI workloads, Cobalt 200 VMs will represent a significant share of new Azure Compute capacity beginning in 2027. Explore Cobalt 200 VM sizes and deployment guidance For customers like Amadeus, Databricks, InMobi, OpenAI, and Snowflake, Cobalt 200 VMs deliver improved performance and efficiency over Cobalt 100 VMs. As a result, customers can deliver faster search results, more responsive database queries, and run their services at higher utilization with fewer cores. Cobalt 200’s performance and efficiency gains reflect our systems approach to infrastructure design, which co-optimizes silicon, software, networking, power, and rack infrastructure. Cobalt 200 VMs are also designed for agentic AI workflows, including agent sandboxes, file search, code compilation, and tool execution, where higher per-core performance can help reduce latency. As customer need for high-performance and low-latency compute increases, we’re adding new virtual machine types to bring the price-performance benefits of Cobalt to additional workloads: Mpsv4 for high memory workloads. entries.summary: Discover how continuous improvement in Microsoft Foundry helps organizations evaluate, optimize, and improve agents over time while keeping teams in control.
entries.text: New models ship every few weeks, and your customers ask questions no one planned for. The agents that learn from all of it pull ahead. That’s continuous improvement, and today at Microsoft Ignite we’re bringing it to Microsoft Foundry. To unlock it, you need an end-to-end system where you build agents, give them context, run them, govern them, and improve them over time. And as part of the new Microsoft IQ, Foundry accomplishes two things that only Microsoft can deliver: your unique intelligence stays your advantage, and your agents keep getting better the longer they run. Out of the box, an AI model is exactly the same for you as it is for anyone else. Three things help you improve your agents as your teams accomplish real work. Agents on Foundry get better the more you use them. Foundry lets you feed agent traces and user input back into the system, creating a continuous learning loop that improves the performance of the system over time. Foundry looks across every run for ways to make your agents better. The system finds and tests improvements; shows you how each one trades off across quality, speed, and cost; and then you decide what ships. Foundry provides a range of other capabilities that allow you to improve progressively, from lightweight skill improvements to agent configuration, all the way to training model weights using your data. entries.summary: Microsoft and fal partner to expand video generation in Microsoft Foundry, helping developers bring creative ideas into enterprise applications.
entries.text: Microsoft and fal partner to expand video generation in Microsoft Foundry, helping developers bring creative ideas into enterprise applications. Video workloads do not all start with the same input or aim for the same result. A creative team might explore several interpretations of a written brief. A retailer might turn an approved product image into a short motion concept. An application developer might combine image generation and video generation into a workflow that takes an idea from description to frame to scene. Each scenario brings different requirements for visual quality, motion, creative control, turnaround time, and cost. All of this means that a multi-model solution is necessary to realize a full vision. Today, Microsoft and fal are helping developers find the right tools for their workloads. We are excited to announce that Kling, LTX, and MiniMax video models are rolling out to in public preview in Microsoft Foundry through our new partnership with fal. Available as a first-party Azure service, these text-to-video and image-to-video options give creators and developers more ways to utilize video generation with the experiences they want to build. The partnership expands the choices available in Microsoft Foundry while bringing video into the broader platform developers use to build AI applications. entries.summary: AI must be selected, architected, and managed as a continuous business discipline, not a series of isolated projects.
entries.text: Transformation begins at the line between an experiment that works and a capability the business depends on. Scaling intelligence requires production capabilities built for sustained business performance, with investments prioritized against financial thresholds, tied to measurable outcomes, instrumented for unit costs, and owned by accountable leaders. This approach manages cost, performance, governance, and reliability as adoption grows. A new IDC InfoBrief, sponsored by Microsoft, Scaling AI Without Scaling Costs*, on how organizations are funding and governing AI, shows both the urgency of that shift and the friction holding it back. Read the IDC InfoBrief Nearly 90% of organizations apply financial thresholds before approving AI initiatives. Scaling AI Without Scaling Costs Only 17% of organizations build models to project how costs scale in production—even as about 78% prioritize cost efficiency when selecting a model. 86% expect financial results within six to 24 months—roughly one budget cycle to show something real. Together, those findings point to a new operating reality: AI must be selected, architected, and managed as a continuous business discipline, not a series of isolated projects. The market has moved from proving it works to proving it can scale economically. entries.summary: Discover how Microsoft is accelerating electronic design automation (EDA) workloads with Azure Cobalt 200 VMs.
entries.text: Azure Cobalt 200 VMs is now generally available. Read more. Every Azure chip Microsoft has built started as electronic design automation (EDA) jobs used to design, test, and validate silicon before it is manufactured. This includes simulation sweeps that run for days, verification regressions that fan out across thousands of cores overnight, and physical signoff runs that use hundreds of gigabytes of memory for a single block. Together, these workloads account for hundreds of millions of compute jobs each year. Today we’re sharing early results from our next step in that evolution: running EDA workloads on Azure Cobalt 200, Azure’s custom compute infrastructure built on the Arm Neoverse CSS V3. In our silicon design environment, the evaluated EDA workloads ran with 1.30x to 4.15x more performance than on Cobalt 100 across a range of testing scenarios, from simulation to verification to static timing analysis. Learn more about Azure Cobalt 200 VMs Traditionally, EDA workloads ran on fixed, on-premise x86 server capacity, sized for peak demand with periods of underutilization. The shift to cloud-based EDA on Microsoft Azure offered a new level of flexibility, scale, and reliability on compute-intensive silicon design workloads. entries.summary: Azure Failure Prediction and Detection (AFPD) helps reduce interruptions by predicting hardware failures, moving eligible workloads, and notifying customers when action is needed.
entries.text: Takeaway: Azure Failure Prediction and Detection (AFPD) is Microsoft Azure’s end-to-end system aiming to catch hardware failures before they interrupt a workload, not after. Across the Azure fleet, AFPD has improved the prevention of hardware-related VM interruptions by 36%. SAP workloads offer a compelling example of AFPD’s value, illustrating why preventing interruptions matters for mission-critical services. But AFPD isn’t specific to SAP: it operates across General Purpose, Specialized Compute, HPC/AI, and select Storage workloads, making SAP’s experience a window into Azure’s broader approach to reliability for mission-critical third-party services. To learn more, watch our companion video to learn how AFPD helps reduce the risk of failures disrupting your critical workloads. Reliability engineered into the platform Most conversations about cloud reliability focus on what you build: zone-redundant architectures, failover patterns, and backup strategies. Less visible, but just as consequential, is what the platform does on your behalf; before a failure ever becomes an incident you need to respond to. That’s the premise behind AFPD, which became fully operational in 2024. AFPD is an end-to-end system that uses machine learning and telemetry to predict, mitigate, and remediate hardware failures in the Azure fleet before they interrupt your workloads.
